subtopics.title: Software Characteristics & Quality Attributes
subtopics.subtitle: Nature of software, the software crisis, McCall and ISO 25010 quality, legacy evolution

concepts.text: What Software Is

Software is the set of programs, data structures and documentation that together make a computer do useful work. Software engineering is the disciplined, quantifiable application of engineering principles to the development, operation and maintenance of software (IEEE definition). Because software is a logical rather than a physical product, it behaves very differently from hardware, and those differences explain why it needs its own engineering discipline.
Classic characteristics of software (Pressman):
items: Software is developed or engineered, not manufactured: the cost is in design and development, and making copies costs almost nothing.
Software does not wear out: it has no physical parts that degrade, but it deteriorates because every change can introduce new defects.
Most software is still custom-built, although component-based reuse (libraries, frameworks, services) is increasing.
Software is complex, intangible (cannot be seen or touched), malleable (easy to change, hence easy to damage) and conforms to arbitrary human rules rather than physical laws.

concepts.text: Failure Curves: Wear Out vs Deterioration

rows: Bathtub: infant mortality, flat useful life, wear-out
Idealised: high early failures then flat; actual curve has spikes
Side effects of changes made during maintenance
No spare parts; every defect is a design error to fix
Failure rate rises at end of life
Minimum failure rate slowly rises with each change

concepts.text: The Software Crisis

In the 1960s, growing hardware power allowed far larger programs than informal methods could handle. Projects ran over budget and schedule, delivered unreliable code that did not meet user needs, and were very hard to maintain. The 1968 NATO conference at Garmisch popularised the term software engineering as the response to this software crisis. Many of the same symptoms still appear today when process, requirements and quality are neglected.
McCall's Quality Factors (1977)

rows: How easy is it to change?
How easy is it to move or reuse?

concepts.text: The syllabus list "CRISP MURTI" defines ten attributes:
items: Correctness: the software satisfies its specification and the user's objectives.
Reliability: it performs its intended function without failure over time; Integrity: it resists unauthorised access or modification.
Efficiency: it uses minimum CPU time, memory and other resources; Usability: effort needed to learn, operate and interpret it.
Maintainability: effort to locate and fix defects; Portability: effort to move it to another platform.
Reusability: parts can be used in other applications; Interoperability: effort to couple it with other systems; Testability: effort to test that it performs its function.

concepts.text: ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010

ISO/IEC 9126 (1991) defined six quality characteristics: functionality, reliability, usability, efficiency, maintainability and portability. It was replaced by ISO/IEC 25010:2011 (the SQuaRE series), whose product quality model has eight characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability. Security and compatibility became top-level characteristics, and 25010 also defines a separate quality-in-use model (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction, freedom from risk, context coverage).

concepts.plainText: Availability A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) = MTTF / MTBF

concepts.text: Legacy Software and Evolution
Legacy systems are older systems still critical to the business; they must evolve because:
items: Adaptive maintenance: the environment changes (new OS, hardware, database or regulations).
Perfective maintenance: users request new features or better performance.
Corrective maintenance: defects discovered in use must be fixed; Preventive maintenance: code is restructured to ease future change.
Maintenance usually consumes the majority of total lifetime cost, commonly quoted as 60 to 80 percent.

concepts.text: Lehman's laws of software evolution describe what happens to programs embedded in the real world (E-type systems). Continuing change says such a system must be continually adapted or it becomes progressively less useful. Increasing complexity says that as a system evolves its structure degrades unless work is done to reduce it. Other laws cover continuing growth of functionality and declining quality unless the system is rigorously maintained.

notes.text: "Software doesn't wear out, it deteriorates" is the favourite characteristic. The actual software failure curve rises in spikes because each maintenance change introduces new defects; hardware follows a bathtub curve.

McCall has 11 factors in 3 perspectives (operation 5, revision 3, transition 3). ISO 9126 has 6 characteristics; ISO/IEC 25010:2011 has 8. The 2023 revision of 25010 adds safety, so always check which edition a question names.

Reliability and availability are different: reliability is the probability of failure-free operation over time, while availability is the fraction of time the system is usable. A system that fails often but recovers instantly can have high availability and low reliability.

formulas.title: Mean time between failures
formulas.description: Average cycle length: mean time the system runs before failing plus the mean time taken to repair it.

formulas.title: Availability
formulas.description: Fraction of time the software is operational and available for use.

formulas.title: Reliability (constant failure rate)
formulas.description: Probability of failure-free operation for time t when failures occur at constant rate lambda = 1/MTTF.

formulas.title: Defect density
formulas.description: Number of defects found per thousand lines of code, a basic quality indicator.

flashcards.front: Why does software deteriorate even though it does not wear out?
flashcards.back: Each change made during maintenance can introduce new defects (side effects), so the minimum failure rate slowly rises over the system's life.

flashcards.front: Name McCall's three quality perspectives and the factors in product revision.
flashcards.back: Product operation, product revision and product transition; revision covers maintainability, flexibility and testability.

flashcards.front: List the eight product quality characteristics of ISO/IEC 25010:2011.
flashcards.back: Functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability.
The 1960s situation where projects were late, over budget, unreliable and hard to maintain; the 1968 NATO conference proposed software engineering as the remedy.

questions.questionText: The actual failure-rate curve of software shows upward spikes during its operational life. What mainly causes these spikes?
options: Physical wear of the storage media holding the program
Side effects introduced by changes made during maintenance
Infant-mortality failures of newly manufactured copies
Rising temperature and dust in the operating environment
questions.explanation: Software has no physical wear; each modification can introduce new defects, causing a spike in failures, and the minimum failure rate creeps upward over time.

questions.questionText: How many product quality characteristics are defined in the ISO/IEC 25010:2011 product quality model?
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 25010:2011 defines 8 characteristics (functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability). ISO 9126 had 6 and McCall has 11 factors.

questions.questionText: In McCall's quality model, which factor belongs to the product transition perspective?
questions.explanation: Product transition contains portability, reusability and interoperability. Testability and maintainability are product revision factors; integrity is a product operation factor.

questions.questionText: Which characteristic distinguishes software from most manufactured hardware products?
options: Its production cost is dominated by raw materials
It is engineered (developed) rather than manufactured, so cost lies in design and development
It follows the bathtub curve and wears out physically
Spare parts can replace a failed software component
questions.explanation: Software is developed or engineered, not manufactured in the classical sense; copies cost almost nothing, so cost concentrates in engineering. It deteriorates through change rather than wearing out.

subtopics.title: Software Process Models: Agile, V, Iterative, Prototype & Big Bang
subtopics.subtitle: Waterfall to Scrum: how each life-cycle model plans, builds, tests and handles change

concepts.text: Software Process and Life-Cycle Models

A software process is a structured set of activities needed to develop a software system. Every process includes four fundamental activities: specification (what the system should do), design and implementation, validation (checking it does what the customer wants) and evolution (changing it as needs change). A process model (SDLC model) is an abstract description of how these activities are ordered and repeated. Plan-driven models fix the plan up front; agile models plan incrementally and embrace change.
Waterfall model (Royce, 1970): phases run strictly in sequence, each producing signed-off documents:
items: Requirements analysis and definition, then system and software design, then implementation and unit testing, then integration and system testing, then operation and maintenance.
Strengths: simple to manage, clear milestones and heavy documentation; suits stable, well-understood requirements and contract-based work.
Weaknesses: rigid; working software appears only late, so requirement errors are found late and are costly to fix.

concepts.text: V-Model (Verification and Validation)

The V-model is an extension of waterfall in which test planning starts during the matching development phase. Verification asks "are we building the product right?" (conformance to specification, via reviews and inspections); validation asks "are we building the right product?" (meeting real user needs, via testing). It still assumes stable requirements and does not produce early prototypes.
Incremental, Iterative and Spiral
Models that deliver or refine the system in repeated cycles:
items: Incremental: requirements are split into increments; each increment is designed, built and delivered, adding functionality to the previous one. Core features arrive first and customers get early value.
Iterative: a skeletal version of the whole system is built first and then refined through repeated cycles of design, build and review, each yielding a working release.

Spiral (Boehm, 1986): risk-driven; each loop passes through four quadrants: determine objectives and constraints, identify and resolve risks (often by prototyping), develop and test, and plan the next loop. Suited to large, high-risk projects.
Radius of the spiral represents cumulative cost; the angular position represents progress in the current loop.

concepts.text: Prototyping, RAD and Big Bang
Models for unclear requirements, tight deadlines or tiny projects:
items: Prototype model: a quick working model is built to clarify ambiguous requirements. Throwaway (rapid) prototypes are discarded after feedback; evolutionary prototypes are refined into the final system.

RAD (Rapid Application Development): very short time-boxed cycles (typically 60 to 90 days) using reusable components, code generators and JAD workshops; phases are requirements planning, user design, construction and cutover.
Big Bang: no formal planning or process; all resources go into coding and the product emerges at the end. Only for very small, academic or experimental work; highly risky and unpredictable.

concepts.text: Agile, Scrum and XP

The Agile Manifesto (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. Agile methods deliver working software in short increments, keep the customer involved and accept changing requirements even late in development.

rows: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers (no traditional project manager)
Sprint (1 month or less, typically 2 to 4 weeks), sprint planning, daily scrum (15 min), sprint review, sprint retrospective
Owns and orders the product backlog; maximises product value
Coaches the team, removes impediments, ensures Scrum is followed

concepts.text: Extreme Programming (XP, Kent Beck) practices:
items: Pair programming, test-first development (TDD), continuous integration and small, frequent releases.
Refactoring, simple design, collective code ownership and coding standards.
On-site customer, user stories for requirements, planning game and a sustainable pace (40-hour week).

concepts.plainText: Sprints needed = ceil(backlog story points / velocity)

rows: Large project with high technical risk
Early partial delivery of core features

formulas.plainText: Velocity = story points completed per sprint
Risk exposure RE = probability x loss

notes.text: Keyword map: risk analysis = spiral; test phase paired with each development phase = V-model; unclear requirements = prototyping; no planning = big bang; sprints and backlog = Scrum; pair programming and TDD = XP; time-box of 60 to 90 days = RAD.

Incremental and iterative are not the same: incremental adds new pieces of functionality in each delivery, while iterative reworks and refines the whole system in each cycle. Many real methods (including Scrum) combine both.

Brooks' law, "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later", follows from ramp-up time and from communication paths growing as n(n - 1)/2 with team size n. Agile keeps teams small (commonly 10 or fewer) for this reason.

formulas.title: Team communication paths
formulas.description: Number of pairwise communication channels in a team of n people, the basis of Brooks' law.

formulas.title: Sprints to finish a backlog
formulas.description: Estimated number of sprints to complete the remaining backlog at the team's measured velocity.

formulas.title: Risk exposure (spiral model)
formulas.description: Probability of a risk occurring times the loss if it occurs, used to rank risks in each spiral loop.

flashcards.front: What are the four quadrants of each loop in Boehm's spiral model?
flashcards.back: Determine objectives, alternatives and constraints; evaluate alternatives and resolve risks; develop and verify the product; plan the next iteration.

flashcards.front: Name the three Scrum artefacts and the five Scrum events.
flashcards.back: Artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, increment. Events: the sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review and sprint retrospective.
A throwaway prototype is discarded once it has clarified requirements; an evolutionary prototype is refined step by step into the delivered system.

flashcards.front: When is the Big Bang model acceptable?
flashcards.back: Only for very small, academic or experimental projects with one or two developers, where the lack of planning carries little risk.

questions.questionText: Which process model explicitly includes a risk analysis and resolution activity in every cycle of development?
questions.explanation: Boehm's spiral model is risk-driven: each loop identifies and resolves the major risks, often by prototyping, before development continues.

questions.questionText: The customer cannot state clear requirements for a new user interface, so the team builds a quick mock-up, gathers feedback and then discards it before building the real system. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: A throwaway (rapid) prototype exists only to clarify requirements and is discarded; an evolutionary prototype is refined into the final product.

questions.questionText: In Scrum, who is accountable for ordering the product backlog to maximise the value of the product?
questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns and orders the product backlog. The Scrum Master coaches and removes impediments, and Scrum has no project manager role.

subtopics.title: Computer-Aided Software Engineering (CASE)
subtopics.subtitle: Upper, lower and integrated CASE, the repository, and forward/reverse engineering tools

concepts.text: What CASE Means

Computer-Aided Software Engineering (CASE) is the use of software tools to support software process activities such as requirements engineering, design, programming, testing, project management and configuration management. CASE tools automate routine work, enforce methods and notations, keep documents consistent with each other and store all project information in a shared repository. The aim is higher productivity and better quality, not replacing engineering judgement.
Classification by Life-Cycle Phase

rows: DFD/ER/UML modelling, requirements managers, prototyping tools
Code generators, compilers, debuggers, test tools, reverse engineering
Upper and lower tools sharing one central repository

concepts.text: Tools classified by the activity they support (Sommerville's functional view):
items: Planning and estimation: PERT/CPM and Gantt tools, cost estimation tools.
Editing and diagramming: text editors, UML and data-flow diagram editors.
Requirements management and change management: traceability tools, issue trackers.
Configuration management: version control and build systems (for example Git and Make).
Prototyping: very high-level languages and user interface generators.
Language processing and program analysis: compilers, static analysers, cross-reference generators.
Testing and debugging: test data generators, file comparators, interactive debuggers.
Documentation and re-engineering: document generators, restructuring and cross-reference tools.

concepts.text: The CASE Repository

The heart of an integrated CASE environment is the repository (also called the data dictionary or encyclopedia). It stores every artefact of the project: requirements, models, data definitions, code, test cases and documents, together with the relationships between them. Because all tools read and write the same repository, a change made in one diagram can be propagated to related diagrams, generated code and documentation, and consistency checks can be run across the whole project.
Integration levels in an I-CASE environment:
items: Data integration: tools share data through the common repository.
Presentation (user-interface) integration: tools share a common look and interaction style.
Control integration: one tool can start or notify another (for example a build triggering tests).
Process integration: the environment embeds knowledge of the process and guides users through its steps.

concepts.text: Tools, Workbenches and Environments

rows: Supports one process phase with a set of tools
Analysis and design workbench, programming IDE
Supports all or most of the process with integrated workbenches

concepts.text: Forward, Reverse and Round-Trip Engineering
CASE tools can move between models and code in both directions:
items: Forward engineering: generate code skeletons or database schemas from design models.
Reverse engineering: analyse existing source code to recover design information such as class diagrams, call graphs and data models.
Re-engineering: reverse engineer a legacy system, restructure or migrate it, then forward engineer the improved version.
Round-trip engineering: keep model and code synchronised so that edits in either are reflected in the other.

concepts.text: Benefits, Limitations and Productivity

rows: Faster, cheaper development of routine parts
Tools may impose a method that does not fit the team
Easier maintenance and reuse via the repository
Cannot fix poor requirements or bad design decisions

notes.text: Upper CASE = front end (requirements, analysis, design); lower CASE = back end (coding, testing, maintenance); I-CASE = whole life cycle through a shared repository. A debugger or test generator is lower CASE; a DFD or UML editor is upper CASE.
Reverse engineering recovers design from code without changing the code; re-engineering goes further and produces an improved system. Forward engineering is the normal model-to-code direction.
CASE tools support a method; they do not supply one. Automating a chaotic process only produces chaos faster, which is why CASE adoption usually follows process improvement.

formulas.title: Development productivity
formulas.description: Thousand lines of code delivered per person-month, used to compare work with and without tools.

formulas.title: Productivity gain from CASE
formulas.description: Percentage improvement in productivity after introducing CASE support.

formulas.title: Return on tool investment
formulas.description: Net benefit of a CASE tool relative to its purchase, training and support cost.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes upper, lower and integrated CASE?
flashcards.back: Upper CASE supports requirements and design, lower CASE supports coding, testing and maintenance, and I-CASE supports the whole life cycle through one repository.
The central database (data dictionary or encyclopedia) holding all project artefacts and their relationships, shared by every tool in an I-CASE environment.
Keeping design models and source code synchronised, so changes in the code update the model and changes in the model regenerate the code.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of a lower CASE tool?
options: Automated test case generator and debugger
questions.explanation: Lower (back-end) CASE supports implementation, testing and maintenance. DFD, ER and requirements tools support early phases and are upper CASE.

questions.questionText: In an integrated CASE environment, the component that stores all project artefacts and lets every tool share them is the:
questions.explanation: The repository, also called the data dictionary or encyclopedia, is the central store that provides data integration across all I-CASE tools.

questions.questionText: Without CASE tools a team delivered 20 KLOC in 40 person-months. With CASE tools a similar 20 KLOC system took 25 person-months. What is the productivity gain?
questions.explanation: Productivity rises from 20/40 = 0.5 to 20/25 = 0.8 KLOC/PM; gain = (0.8 - 0.5)/0.5 = 60%. The 37.5% option is the saving in effort, not the productivity gain.

questions.questionText: A CASE tool reads the source code of an undocumented legacy system and produces class diagrams and call graphs, without modifying the code. This activity is called:
questions.explanation: Reverse engineering recovers design information from existing code. Re-engineering also restructures and rebuilds the system, and forward engineering goes from models to code.

subtopics.title: Functional, Non-Functional, User & System Requirements
subtopics.subtitle: FR vs NFR, domain requirements, product/organisational/external NFRs and interfaces

concepts.text: What a Requirement Is

A requirement is a description of a service the system must provide or a constraint on its operation. Requirements range from abstract, high-level statements for customers to detailed, precise specifications that can serve as part of a contract. Sommerville distinguishes them in two ways: by level of detail (user vs system requirements) and by kind (functional, non-functional and domain requirements).
Functional vs Non-Functional

rows: WHAT the system does: services, reactions to inputs, behaviour
HOW WELL it does it: qualities and constraints
Usually a specific feature or function
Often applies to the system as a whole
The system shall let a student download the admit card
Pages shall load within 2 seconds for 1,000 concurrent users
The whole system may be unusable

concepts.text: Non-functional requirements are often more critical than individual functional ones: an aircraft control system that is not certified as reliable cannot be used at all. They also drive the architecture, because performance, security and availability goals decide how components are distributed and replicated. A single NFR such as a security requirement may generate several related functional requirements, for example a login function and an audit log.
Classification of Non-Functional Requirements

rows: Policies and procedures of customer or developer
Environmental, operational, development (for example must use a given language or process)
Factors outside the system and its development
Regulatory, ethical, legislative (accounting, safety, privacy laws)

concepts.text: Domain requirements come from the application domain rather than a specific user:
items: They reflect fundamental rules of the domain, for example a banking rule for interest calculation or a train-protection deceleration formula.
They may be new functional requirements, constraints on existing ones or specific computations.
Problem: they are written in domain language that software engineers may misunderstand, and domain experts may omit them because they seem obvious.

concepts.text: User vs System Requirements

rows: Structured language, models, tables, formal notation
Abstract statements of services and constraints
Detailed, precise description of functions, services and constraints
Basis for design; may form part of the contract

concepts.text: Problems with natural-language requirements and how to reduce them:
items: Lack of clarity, requirements confusion (functional and non-functional mixed) and requirements amalgamation (several requirements in one sentence).
Use a standard format, use "shall" for mandatory and "should" for desirable requirements, and highlight key terms.
Avoid jargon and give the rationale for each requirement; use structured or form-based templates for system requirements.

concepts.text: Interface Specification and Measurable NFRs

Most systems must work with existing systems, so the requirements must include precise interface specifications. Sommerville lists three types: procedural interfaces (APIs offered by existing programs or subsystems), data structures passed from one subsystem to another, and representations of data such as bit ordering or encoding. Formal notations or programming-language interface definitions are effective because they are precise.

rows: Transactions per second, user or event response time
Training time, number of help frames
MTTF, probability of unavailability, rate of failure occurrence (ROCOF)
Time to restart after failure, probability of data corruption on failure
Percentage of target-dependent statements, number of target systems

concepts.plainText: Downtime per year = (1 - A) x 8760 hours

formulas.plainText: Downtime = (1 - A) x 8760 hours per year

notes.text: Test for an FR: can you describe it as an input and a response ("the system shall calculate...")? Anything about speed, security, reliability, usability, portability, law or company policy is an NFR ("PURPS": performance, usability, reliability, portability, security).
Vague NFRs such as "the system shall be user-friendly" cannot be tested. Rewrite them with a measurable metric, for example "trained users shall make no more than 2 errors per hour".

Legislative and regulatory requirements (privacy law, tax law, safety standards) are external NFRs; rules about the development language or process are organisational NFRs; response time and memory limits are product NFRs.

formulas.title: Allowed downtime from availability
formulas.description: Converts an availability requirement into the maximum permitted downtime per year.

formulas.title: Throughput requirement
formulas.description: Measurable form of a speed requirement, stating how many transactions must be processed per unit time.

formulas.title: Probability of failure on demand
formulas.description: Reliability metric for systems used on demand, such as a protection system.

flashcards.front: What are Sommerville's three classes of non-functional requirement?
flashcards.back: Product requirements, organisational requirements and external requirements (regulatory, ethical and legislative).
A requirement derived from the application domain, such as a standard formula or industry rule, rather than from a specific user's needs.

flashcards.front: Which three types of interface must be specified in the requirements?
flashcards.back: Procedural interfaces (APIs), data structures passed between subsystems, and representations of data such as bit ordering.
User requirements are abstract natural-language statements for customers; system requirements are detailed, precise specifications for developers and can form part of the contract.

questions.questionText: Requirements that come from the application area of the system, such as a standard formula used in railway braking, rather than from a particular user's needs are called:
questions.explanation: Domain requirements reflect the rules and characteristics of the application domain and can be functional requirements or constraints on them.

questions.questionText: "The system shall not disclose any personal data of citizens except as permitted by the national privacy act." Under Sommerville's classification this is a(n):
questions.explanation: It is imposed by a law outside the system and its development process, so it is an external, legislative non-functional requirement.

questions.questionText: An NFR states that the online exam system shall have 99.9% availability. What is the maximum downtime allowed in a year of 8,760 hours?
questions.explanation: Downtime = (1 - 0.999) x 8760 = 0.001 x 8760 = 8.76 hours per year.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the interface types that Sommerville says must be specified when a new system works with existing subsystems?
options: Representations of data such as bit ordering
questions.explanation: The three interface types are procedural interfaces, data structures and data representations. A training schedule is a project plan item, not an interface specification.

subtopics.title: Requirements Engineering: Elicitation, Analysis, SRS, Validation & Management
subtopics.subtitle: Feasibility, elicitation techniques, IEEE 830 SRS, validation checks and traceability

concepts.text: The Requirements Engineering Process

Requirements engineering (RE) is the process of finding out, analysing, documenting and checking the services and constraints of a system. Its main activities are the feasibility study, requirements elicitation and analysis, requirements specification and requirements validation, with requirements management running alongside throughout the project. In practice these activities are interleaved and iterated, often drawn as a spiral in which each round adds more detail.

rows: Can it be built with available technology and skills?
Do the benefits justify the cost (cost-benefit analysis)?
Does it violate any law, licence or regulation?
Will the organisation and its users actually use it?
Can it be delivered within the required time?

concepts.text: Elicitation and Analysis
Sommerville's elicitation and analysis cycle:
items: Requirements discovery: interacting with stakeholders to collect their requirements, including domain requirements.
Classification and organisation: grouping related requirements into coherent clusters.
Prioritisation and negotiation: resolving conflicts between stakeholders and ranking requirements (for example MoSCoW: must, should, could, won't).
Specification: documenting the requirements as input to the next round.

rows: Structured or free-form questioning of stakeholders
Analyst watches real work in context
Tacit, social and actual work practices
Facilitated group workshops with users and developers
Users try a mock-up and give feedback

concepts.text: Elicitation is hard because stakeholders often do not know what they want, express requirements in their own terms, have conflicting needs, and are influenced by organisational politics. Requirements also change during analysis as the business environment changes. Combining several techniques, for example interviews plus observation plus prototyping, gives a more complete picture than any one alone.
The Software Requirements Specification (SRS)

The SRS is the official statement of what the developers must implement and often serves as a contract between customer and developer. It should say what the system does, not how it is designed. IEEE Std 830-1998 is the classic template; it has been superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, which keeps essentially the same content.

rows: Purpose, scope, definitions and abbreviations, references, overview
Product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, constraints, assumptions and dependencies
External interfaces, functional requirements, performance, logical database, design constraints, software system attributes

concepts.text: IEEE 830 qualities of a good SRS:
items: Correct (every requirement is one the software must meet) and unambiguous (only one interpretation).
Complete (all significant requirements, responses to all inputs, labelled figures and defined terms) and consistent (no conflicting requirements).
Ranked for importance and/or stability, and verifiable (a cost-effective finite process can check each requirement).
Modifiable (structured so changes are easy and not duplicated) and traceable (origin of each requirement is clear and it can be referenced forward).

concepts.text: Validation and Management
Requirements validation checks that the requirements define the system the customer really wants:
items: Checks: validity (right functions), consistency (no conflicts), completeness (all functions and constraints), realism (achievable within budget and technology) and verifiability (testable).
Techniques: requirements reviews (systematic manual analysis), prototyping (executable model shown to users) and test-case generation (a requirement that cannot be tested is flawed).
Errors found here are far cheaper to fix than errors found after delivery.

concepts.text: Requirements management controls change to requirements throughout the project:
items: Enduring requirements are stable and tied to the core domain; volatile requirements change (mutable, emergent, consequential, compatibility).

Traceability: backward traceability links a requirement to its source (stakeholder, document); forward traceability links it to design, code and tests. The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) records these links.

Change management: problem analysis and change specification, change analysis and costing (impact analysis using traceability), then change implementation, usually approved by a change control board (CCB).

notes.text: Remember the SRS qualities as CUCVM-T plus ranked: correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable, modifiable, traceable, ranked for importance/stability. "The system shall be fast" fails verifiability because no test can decide it.
Validation checks are validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability. Realism means the requirement can be implemented with the available budget, schedule and technology.
An SRS should state what the system must do, not how it will be built. Design decisions inside an SRS over-constrain the developers and make the document harder to change.

Pressman's metrics: Q1 = n_ui/n_r is specificity (lack of ambiguity), where n_ui is the number of requirements every reviewer interpreted identically and n_r the total; Q2 = n_u/(n_i x n_s) is completeness of functional requirements, where n_u is unique function requirements, n_i inputs and n_s states.

formulas.title: Requirement specificity
formulas.description: Fraction of requirements that all reviewers interpreted identically; closer to 1 means less ambiguity.

formulas.title: Functional completeness
formulas.description: Unique function requirements divided by the number of inputs times states specified.

formulas.title: Requirements volatility
formulas.description: Percentage of requirements added, deleted or modified over a period, a measure of requirements stability.

formulas.title: Traceability coverage
formulas.description: Percentage of requirements linked in the RTM to design, code and test cases.

flashcards.front: What are the three main sections of an IEEE 830 SRS?
flashcards.back: 1 Introduction, 2 Overall description, and 3 Specific requirements, followed by appendices and an index.

flashcards.front: List the five requirements validation checks.
flashcards.back: Validity, consistency, completeness, realism and verifiability.
Backward traceability links a requirement to its source stakeholder or document; forward traceability links it to the design elements, code and tests that implement it.

flashcards.front: What does TELOS stand for in a feasibility study?
flashcards.back: Technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule feasibility.

questions.questionText: During a feasibility study, the analyst checks whether the clerks in the ministry will accept and actually use the proposed system in their daily work. This is:
questions.explanation: Operational feasibility asks whether the system will work in the organisation and be used by its people; technical, economic and schedule feasibility examine technology, cost-benefit and time.

questions.questionText: In the IEEE 830 SRS template, the detailed functional requirements, external interface requirements and performance requirements are placed in:
questions.explanation: Section 3 (Specific requirements) holds the detailed requirements; section 2 gives only a general overview of product functions, users and constraints.

questions.questionText: An SRS contains the statement "The report screen shall appear quickly." No test can decide whether this is met. Which SRS quality is most directly violated?
questions.explanation: A requirement is verifiable only if a finite, cost-effective process can check it; "quickly" has no measurable criterion, such as a response time in seconds.

questions.questionText: An SRS has 40 requirements. After review, all reviewers interpreted 30 of them identically. What is Pressman's specificity metric Q1?
questions.explanation: Q1 = n_ui / n_r = 30 / 40 = 0.75; the closer Q1 is to 1, the less ambiguous the specification.

questions.questionText: During requirements validation, a reviewer checks whether a requirement can be implemented with the available budget, schedule and technology. Which validation check is this?
questions.explanation: The realism check confirms that requirements are achievable given budget, schedule and technology; consistency looks for conflicts and validity asks whether the functions are the right ones.
